entries.title: The Light in the Storm
entries.body:
On a rocky cape by the sea stood an old lighthouse. In it lived a keeper named Jakob, who lit the great lamp every evening. Its light reached far out over the waves and showed the ships the way past the dangerous rocks.

One wild night a storm broke out like nothing Jakob had ever known. The wind howled, the rain beat against the windows, and the waves crashed against the rocks. In the middle of the darkness, Jakob suddenly saw a small fishing boat struggling with the waves. The people on board could not find the way to the harbour.

Jakob knew what he had to do. All night he stood by the light and made sure it did not go out. Whenever the flame flickered, he built it up again. He was tired and chilled to the bone, but he did not give up.

Toward morning the storm died down. The fishing boat sailed safely into the harbour. The people on board said that, without the lighthouse's light, they would have been lost in the dark night. Jakob smiled and, weary, went off to rest. His light had once again guided someone home.

On land they walk slowly and waddle from side to side. On the ice they often throw themselves onto their tummies and slide, which looks very funny. Parents care for their chicks together and keep them warm under their own warm tummies.

entries.title: The Hidden City in the Clouds
entries.body:
High in the mountains of South America, among clouds and steep peaks, hides the ancient stone city of Machu Picchu. It lies in the country of Peru, on top of a steep mountain ledge, kilometres above the valley below.

The city was built more than five hundred years ago by the Inca, a people who once ruled a great part of South America. Out of large stones they built houses, stairways and terraces. They cut and fitted the stones so precisely that even today you cannot slide a sheet of paper between them — and all without any mortar to hold them together.

Then something strange happened. The people left the city, and for long centuries Machu Picchu lay hidden from the world, overgrown with forest and wrapped in mist. Only a little more than a hundred years ago was it found again, and the world was amazed at its beauty.

Today thousands of visitors climb the steep path up to Machu Picchu every year. When they step among the old walls, high above the clouds, they feel just how skilled and wise the builders of this mysterious city must have been.

entries.title: Why Food Has Flavour
entries.body: The tongue detects basic tastes such as sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and savoury. Much of flavour also comes from smell. Odour molecules can reach the nose from food in the mouth as well as from food held near it. The brain combines these messages with information about texture and temperature. entries.title: The Travelling Drop
entries.body: Water continually moves between land, oceans, and air. Sunlight warms liquid water and some becomes invisible water vapour. Higher in the air, cooling vapour forms tiny droplets that gather into clouds. Rain or snow returns water to the surface, where it may soak into soil or flow toward rivers. This water cycle reuses the same water while moving it through many places and forms. A drying puddle has not lost its water into nothing. Molecules have escaped into the air as water vapour. That vapour is invisible, unlike the tiny droplets or ice crystals that make up clouds. After rain falls, its path is not always a quick trip into a river. Some soaks into the ground, some is taken up by plants, and some remains in lakes or freezes. Water can spend very different lengths of time in these places. Drawing several arrows from a rain-soaked patch of ground is therefore more accurate than drawing only one. The cycle is a network of routes, powered in large part by sunlight and shaped by gravity and living things.

The rain had not stopped all day. Mia sat by the window and watched the drops run down the glass, when a thin sound came from the garden. It was not the rain. It was a tiny, frightened meow.

entries.title: Hunting in the Dark
entries.body:
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Their wings are not made of feathers but of thin skin, stretched between very long fingers. By day, bats sleep hanging upside down in caves or hollow trees. When the sun goes down, they wake up and set off to hunt.

It is dark, but a bat does not need much light. As it flies, it sends out short, high calls. The sounds are so high that our ears cannot hear them. When a call hits a moth or a mosquito, an echo bounces back. From the echo the bat knows exactly where the insect is, how big it is and which way it is moving. Then it snaps it up in the air.

A small bat can catch hundreds of insects in a single night. Every one of them might have bitten you.

entries.title: Seeing with Sound
entries.body:
Deep water is often dark and cloudy, and eyes are not much help there. Yet dolphins find fish with ease, even at night. Their secret is sound.

A dolphin sends out fast clicks from the front of its head. The clicks travel through the water, hit whatever lies ahead and bounce back as echoes. From these echoes the dolphin builds a picture of its surroundings: a rock, a sunken ship, a shoal of fish. It can tell how far away a fish is, how big it is and in which direction it is swimming. It is a little like seeing with your ears.

Dolphins also hunt as a team. A pod will circle a shoal of fish and drive it together into a tight ball, so that every dolphin can dart in and grab a meal.

Because a dolphin is a mammal, it breathes air. It comes up, blows out a puff of spray through the hole on top of its head, takes a quick breath and dives again. A dolphin can stay under for around ten minutes, but usually it comes up far sooner.

entries.title: The Largest Animal of All
entries.body:
The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, heavier than any dinosaur. A grown blue whale can be thirty metres long, longer than two buses in a row. Its heart is the size of a small car, and its tongue alone weighs as much as an elephant.

You might think such a giant eats giant food. In fact it eats some of the smallest creatures in the sea: krill, tiny shrimp-like animals no longer than your finger. The whale swims into a swarm of krill with its mouth wide open, takes in a huge gulp of water and pushes it out again through the comb-like plates in its mouth. The krill stay behind and are swallowed. In one day a blue whale can eat around four tonnes of them.

When it comes up to breathe, the whale blows a cloud of spray high into the air, as high as a house with three floors. People on whale-watching boats often see this spout long before they see the whale itself.

entries.title: The Stone Faces of Rapa Nui
entries.body:
Far out in the Pacific Ocean, far from any other land, lies a small island called Rapa Nui. Most people know it as Easter Island. Along its green coast stand hundreds of huge stone figures with long faces and heavy brows. They are called moai.

The people of Rapa Nui carved them from volcanic rock many centuries ago, using only stone tools. Some moai are taller than a house and weigh more than ten elephants. How were they moved across the island? Nobody knows for certain. Many islanders say the statues “walked”. Scientists have shown that people with ropes can rock a standing statue forward step by step, so perhaps the old stories are true.

Today the moai stand quietly with their backs to the sea, looking over the island as they have done for hundreds of years.

entries.title: The Red Rock in the Desert
entries.body:

Uluru changes colour with the light. At sunrise and sunset it glows deep orange and red; in the rain it turns silver-grey, and waterfalls pour down its sides. Around its base grow desert oaks and grasses, and there are waterholes where birds and kangaroos come to drink.

For the Anangu, the Aboriginal people who have lived here for tens of thousands of years, Uluru is a sacred place. Visitors are no longer allowed to climb it; they walk around the rock instead and listen to the stories of the people who know it best.

entries.title: A City Standing on a Forest
entries.body:
Imagine a city where the streets are made of water. That city is Venice, in the north of Italy. It is built on more than a hundred islands in a shallow lagoon, and about four hundred bridges tie the islands together.

How can heavy stone houses stand on soft, muddy islands? Long ago the Venetians drove millions of wooden poles into the mud, close together like the bristles of a brush, and built on top of them. The mud kept the air away from the wood, so it never rotted. Over the centuries it became almost as hard as stone. Venice is standing on a forest turned upside down.

There are no cars in Venice. People walk, or they take a boat. The water buses are called vaporetti; ambulances and fire engines are boats, and even the rubbish is collected by boat. The famous black gondolas are mostly for visitors today.

Venice has one big worry: the sea. Several times a year high tides flood the lowest squares, and the city is slowly sinking. Huge gates at the entrance to the lagoon now close when a flood is coming.

entries.title: The Amazon Rainforest
entries.body:
The Amazon rainforest is the largest forest on Earth. It covers a huge part of South America, across nine countries, and through it winds the Amazon River, which carries more water than any other river in the world.

It is warm and wet here all year round. Rain falls almost every day. The tallest trees rise sixty metres above the ground and form a green roof called the canopy. Most of the forest’s animals live up there rather than on the dark forest floor.

Nowhere else on Earth are there so many kinds of living things. Monkeys swing through the branches, toucans crack fruit with their enormous beaks, and scarlet macaws fly screeching over the treetops. Bright blue butterflies as large as a hand drift between the trunks, tiny tree frogs cling to the leaves, and the jaguar, the biggest cat in the Americas, hunts silently below.

The forest matters to the whole world. Its billions of trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and they help to make rain that falls far away. That is why so many people are working to protect it.

entries.body: Long before there were clocks, people told the time by the sun. A sundial is the simplest clock of all: a stick standing in the ground. entries.title: Life Between the Tides
entries.body:
Twice a day the sea rises up the shore, and twice a day it slides back again. These movements are called tides. They are caused mainly by the Moon, whose gravity pulls the water of the oceans towards it as the Earth turns.

When the tide goes out, some water stays behind in hollows between the rocks. These are tide pools, full of life. A sea anemone looks like a flower, but it is an animal; its soft arms catch tiny creatures that drift too close. Crabs hide under stones, snails scrape green weed off the rocks, and small fish dart between them.

Life in a tide pool is not easy. For hours the water grows warm in the sun, then the waves crash back. The anemone pulls in its arms, the mussels close their shells tight, and everyone waits until the sea returns.

entries.title: Moving a Mountain of Stone
entries.body:
The Great Pyramid of Egypt is made of more than two million blocks of stone. Many of them weigh as much as two cars. The builders had no cranes and no machines. How did they do it?

The blocks were cut in a quarry and laid on wooden sledges. Teams of workers pulled the sledges with thick ropes. A worker in front poured water on the sand. Wet sand is firm and smooth, so the sledge slid along much more easily. To lift the blocks higher as the pyramid grew, the builders made long ramps of earth for the sledges. With wooden levers they nudged each block into its final place.

A ramp, a lever and a sledge are simple machines: they make heavy work easier. The Egyptians used them so well that their pyramid has stood for four and a half thousand years.

entries.title: The Journey of a River
entries.body:
High in the mountains, where the snow melts, a river is born. At first it is only a trickle between the rocks. Other trickles join it, and soon a young stream is racing downhill, leaping down as a waterfall and carrying stones, sand and mud.

All this rushing water is hard at work. Year after year it grinds away at the rock and cuts a valley deeper and deeper. The stones it carries are rolled and knocked together into smooth, round pebbles.

In the flat lowlands the river slows down and begins to wander in curves. Here it drops much of the sand and mud it has carried, and the land beside it becomes rich soil for fields. People build villages and bridges along its banks, and herons wait in the shallows for fish.

At last the river reaches the sea. Fresh water mixes with salt water, and the last of the sand settles into a beach. The sun lifts water from the sea as vapour, the wind carries it back to the mountains as clouds, and there it falls as rain and snow. The journey begins again.

entries.title: Why Ice Floats
entries.body:
When winter comes, the pond freezes first, then the lake, and last of all the river. Moving water is hard to freeze. It freezes at the edges, where it flows slowly, and the ice creeps out from the banks a little further each cold night. Where the current is strong, the river stays open, and sheets of ice break off and float away downstream.

Why do they float? Ice is lighter than water. Almost everything gets smaller and heavier when it turns solid, but water is different: as it freezes, its tiny particles line up in an open pattern, so ice takes up more room and floats on top. The ice on a river forms a lid that keeps the water underneath from freezing, and fish and frogs survive the winter below it.

Tom and his dog watch the ice drift past. River ice is never safe to walk on. It may look thick, but water moves under it and wears it thin in places. In spring the sun warms it, the ice cracks with loud bangs, and the river carries the broken pieces away to the sea.

entries.body: We cannot see the wind. But we can see what it does. It pushes the clouds across the sky. It turns the big white wind turbines on the hill. They make electricity for the village.

entries.title: The Squirrel’s Winter Store
entries.body: In autumn the red squirrel is very busy. It collects acorns, nuts and seeds and buries them in the ground. It hides them in many different places. In winter there is little to eat, so the squirrel digs up its stores. It does not remember every hiding place. Some nuts stay in the ground. In spring they grow into new oak trees.

entries.title: White in Winter
entries.body: The arctic fox lives in the far north. Its fur is thick and warm. In summer the fur is brown or grey. In winter it turns white, so the fox is hard to see in the snow. When it is very cold, the fox wraps its bushy tail around its body like a scarf. Above it, the northern lights glow in the sky.

entries.title: Where Rain Comes From
entries.body: Where does rain come from? When the sun warms a lake or the sea, some of the water turns into vapour and rises into the air. High up it is cold, and the vapour turns back into tiny drops of water. Millions of drops make a cloud. Inside the cloud they bump into each other and join up. When a drop has grown big and heavy enough, the air can no longer hold it, and it falls as rain. The rain soaks into the soil, where the plants are waiting for it.

entries.title: Flying South
entries.body: Every autumn, when the days grow shorter and the first frost comes, the wild geese leave. They fly in a long line shaped like the letter V. The bird at the front works hardest, because it cuts through the air for the others. When it gets tired, it drops back and another goose takes the lead. They travel thousands of kilometres to warmer lands, where they can find food all winter. In spring, when the snow melts at home, they fly all the way back to the same lakes and fields.

entries.title: The Hedgehog’s Long Sleep
entries.body:
When the sun goes down, the hedgehog wakes up. All night it snuffles through the garden looking for beetles, worms, snails and slugs. A gardener is glad to have one, because it eats the slugs that eat the lettuce.

A hedgehog has about five thousand spines on its back. They are stiff, and when a fox comes too close, the hedgehog rolls itself into a tight ball. Only the spines point outwards. Most foxes give up.

In late autumn the hedgehog eats as much as it can and grows fat. Then it builds a nest of dry leaves under a hedge or a pile of wood and falls into a deep winter sleep. Its heart slows down from nearly two hundred beats a minute to about twenty, and its body grows cold. It sleeps like this until spring, living only on its fat.

entries.title: Why Leaves Change Colour
entries.body:
In autumn the days grow shorter and the nights turn cold. All summer the leaves have been green, because they are full of a green colouring called chlorophyll, which uses sunlight to make food for the tree. Now the tree stops making it. As the green fades, the yellow and orange that were hiding in the leaf all along come out, and some trees make a fiery red as well.

Autumn is also harvest time. The apples are ripe, red and sweet. Mia and Tom carry a full basket home across the old wooden bridge, while a squirrel on the railing stuffs its cheeks with acorns for the winter.

Soon the leaves will let go and drift down onto the stream. The tree does not need them any more. It will rest through the winter and grow new ones when spring returns.

entries.title: The Web Beneath the Forest
entries.body:
After a few days of autumn rain, mushrooms appear in the forest as if by magic: brown ones with fat stems, and the famous red one with white spots. But a mushroom is only the tip of something much bigger.

Under the leaves and soil, the real fungus spreads out as a web of fine white threads. The mushroom is just its fruit, pushed up above the ground to scatter tiny spores on the wind.

The threads do a job the forest could not manage without. They wrap around the roots of the trees and trade with them: the fungus passes the tree water and minerals from the soil, and the tree pays with sugar it has made in its leaves. Many trees in a forest are linked to each other through the same fungus, so scientists sometimes call it the wood wide web. Fungi also break down dead leaves and fallen trunks, turning them back into soil.

Some mushrooms are delicious and some are deadly. The red one in the picture is poisonous. Never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has checked it.

entries.title: Why We Have Seasons
entries.body:
Spring, summer, autumn, winter, and then spring again. But why do we have seasons at all?

The Earth travels around the Sun once a year. As it goes, it spins like a top, but the top is tilted a little to one side. So for part of the year, the northern half of the Earth leans towards the Sun. The Sun then climbs high in the sky, the days are long, and its rays hit the ground almost straight on, so they warm it strongly. That is our summer. Half a year later the same half leans away from the Sun. The Sun stays low, the days are short, and its rays arrive at a slant and spread their warmth thinly. That is winter.

Because the two halves of the Earth lean in opposite directions, the seasons are swapped: when children in Europe build snowmen, children in Australia are at the beach. Near the equator, in the middle, the tilt makes little difference, and it is warm all year round. Spring and autumn are the in-between times, when neither half leans much towards the Sun.
